title: Strategic Decision Focused Learning
claim: Prior learning paradigms stop at prediction or action, or loop back via distribution shift; ours adds a strategic response without a feedback loop.
layout: 4 side-by-side vertical flowcharts, top-to-bottom, ours highlighted in green with star badge
description: Four tall panels sit side by side, each a vertical stack of grey boxes joined by short downward arrows. Panel 1, Standard Training, has Data, ML Model and Prediction. Panel 2, Decision-Focused Learning, has Data, ML Model, Prediction and Action. Panel 3, Strategic DFL, is the proposed setting. It has a green tint and a green border, a bold green title and a green 'ours ★' badge. It has Data, ML Model, Prediction, Action and Strategic Response. Panel 4, Performative Prediction, has the same five boxes as panel 3 plus Distribution Shift. A thick black arrow runs from Distribution Shift back up to Data, forming a feedback loop. Panel 3 has no such loop. The green panel draws the eye first. Each pipeline grows longer from left to right.
caption: Comparison of different learning paradigms. In contrast to classical and decision-focused learning, SDFL operates in a strategic context, significantly complicating the learning task. Unlike performative prediction or strategic classification, the data distribution is exogenous—free from strategic feedback loops.
abstract: Machine learning (ML) predictions are increasingly being used to guide decision-making, giving rise to the problem of decision-focused learning (DFL) where predictors are optimized for downstream decision quality rather than accuracy alone. However, most existing work assumes a single decision-maker optimizing in isolation. This paper formalizes strategic decision-focused learning, where an ML system predicts an exogenous state that some agents observe before playing a game. For example, a park ranger may predict wildlife locations to allocate anti-poaching patrols against strategic poachers. While the exogenous state is unaffected by agent actions, predictions influence agents' strategies and the resulting equilibrium. We find that strategic considerations fundamentally change the learning problem. In particular, we show the prediction accuracy-equilibrium payoff landscape can be non-monotonic, i.e., better predictions can degrade performance. We propose algorithmic approaches to address these challenges and validate them across benchmarks in wildlife conservation and infrastructure protection. Our theory and experiments highlight the importance of accounting for strategic interactions when designing predictors.
